title: Hadjar insists Red Bull don’t have ‘the fastest car’
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar believes that Red Bull do not “have the fastest car” despite their triumphs in Malaysia and Singapore, with the Frenchman labelling Ferrari as the quickest team on the grid last time out.

While Max Verstappen had the opportunity to capitalise on Red Bull’s major upgrades and secure two long-awaited wins, Hadjar was held back by problems with the car that were out of his control.

A series of technical issues in Singapore prevented him from partaking in Sprint Qualifying and forced the team to make changes to the power unit, which relegated him to a pit lane start for the Grand Prix before he charged to P10.

The contrasting fortunes between the team mates were obvious, but Hadjar refuted any suggestion that Verstappen’s performances proved that Red Bull now have the fastest car heading into the final races.

Speaking ahead of the United States Grand Prix, he said: “No. I don't think we have the fastest car.

“I think the car is still very hard to drive. In Malaysia it was dominant, but I don’t think in Singapore it was the fastest car. That’s what I believe. I think if you put Max in the Ferrari, he would’ve won the race with more margin – that’s my opinion. In Singapore, I think [Ferrari] was the fastest car.

“[Verstappen] qualified on pole by half a tenth. Ferrari didn’t have new tyres in the race – I mean, not the softs. This has an effect as well. He put all the chances on his side, he made the difference in Q3 and that was enough.”

Although he didn’t have the best luck in Singapore, Hadjar was eager to leave the frustrations behind him and focus on delivering a strong result at the Circuit of The Americas, where he finished P16 for Racing Bulls last season.

“It was one of those weekends where you get a failure in each session,” Hadjar reflected. “You learn from it and we just move on. I’m happy to be here in Texas. I like the track and the car – performance-wise – has been working really well these last couple of weekends.

“We’re confident as a team but of course we are aware of the upgrades in the other garages. We’re still down to earth and we still know our weaknesses on the car.

“We’re still working on it. I just want to go out there and have another clean one because the last two weekends have been very frustrating considering the car I’ve been given.”

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was also questioned about Red Bull’s position in the pecking order and readily admitted that their upgrades have enabled them to catch up to the other frontrunners.

“I think Red Bull definitely took a pretty big step forward over the last triple header,” the Australian said. “Whatever upgrades they put on the car in Baku were very strong – obviously they had a double podium there, and then won the next two races with Max.

“It wasn’t a surprise that Ferrari were very strong in Singapore. On the data analysis, they’re always the joint-quickest or outright quickest in basically every corner this year, but they lose on all the straights – whether that’s from drag, from power, I don’t know.

“We certainly expected Ferrari to be the benchmark in Singapore, but we’ve expected them to be the benchmark at other circuits and it’s not turned out to be the case. I think they're very strong.

“Clearly the Red Bull was very strong. Both are stronger than us, for sure. I think over the last few weeks, Red Bull have definitely become the most consistently quick car, but I think each weekend the challenges are rotating.”

title: When Taylor Swift performed at the United States GP weekend
excerpt:
This year marks a decade since Taylor Swift performed at the United States Grand Prix, and helped Austin become one of that season’s biggest events. The international pop star helped pull in huge crowds at the Circuit of The Americas – including plenty of ‘Swifties’ – and the love for the hitmaker has been felt far and wide in the paddock since.

For Swift, the 2016 United States Grand Prix would be only her second performance that year – and her only public show – after appearing at the Grammys in February. After a hugely popular 1989 album world tour in 2015, Swift wanted time to rest and recover, but an invitation from COTA’s race organisers certainly got her interest.

The United States Grand Prix has long embraced its Texas roots, from cowboy hats in the paddock to special Stetson podium hats for the top three drivers.

As someone who began her career as a country star, Swift felt like the ideal headliner for the entertainment, and ticket sales reflected that. A Saturday general admission ticket gained you access to Qualifying and the huge stage show later on in the evening. For a racing fan who’s also a Swiftie, of which there are many, it was the ultimate crossover.

The 15-song set drew an estimated crowd of around 80,000 people, helping deliver a welcome boost for the organisers.

Long before Drive to Survive introduced many new fans to F1, Swift's appearance offered an example of how major entertainment acts could bring fresh audiences to the sport.

How COTA became a blueprint for circuits

In only its fifth year, Circuit of The Americas had secured one of the world’s biggest music stars to perform over the race weekend – offering fans a ticket to excellent racing action but also a super show in the evening.

“I think at that moment, not many Formula 1 tracks were doing the ‘concert model’ and a lot of circuits were focused on more of the racing side, as opposed to the whole fan event that goes around it – which is very much the norm nowadays,” F1 journalist Luke Smith of The Athletic explained to F1.com.

“COTA was very much ahead of the curve, and it managed to tap into that younger, more female audience that, again, in F1 nowadays is very much the norm,” Smith continued.

“We have seen that big shift happen since the Liberty takeover in the last five to ten years. The boom of Drive to Survive has played a big part in that, but I think that the route of having the concert did help open F1 up to a wave of new fans who perhaps came to the circuit chiefly for the concert and then became interested in F1 because of that.

“COTA has been one of the tracks leading the way on that. They do really put a lot of effort into ensuring that it is a festival around what is happening on the circuit and it’s not just a race, which is a blueprint and a model that a lot of other circuits have followed.”

The Swifties of the F1 paddock

Several drivers have shown their support for the Shake It Off singer in recent years, from including her hits in their pre-race playlists to going with family and friends to the Eras Tour.

Both Pierre Gasly and Charles Leclerc attended the 2024 tour in Milan, with their respective partners – with both drivers declaring themselves fans of her music.

At one of her Wembley shows in London, George Russell showed his support with his niece and even sported a pink fluffy cowboy hat for the occasion.

Ollie Bearman also had five Swift songs in his Apple Music playlist that was shared earlier this year, including ...Ready For It?, Bad Blood, Cruel Summer and Love Story.

Nearly a decade later, concerts have become an established part of many Grand Prix weekends, while F1's audience has continued to expand. Swift's appearance at COTA offered an early glimpse of how music and motorsport could combine to create a wider fan experience.

title: Slater to make FP1 debut with Audi in Mexico City and Sao Paulo
excerpt:
Audi Development Driver Freddie Slater will get his first taste of Formula 1 race weekend action when he drives for Audi in FP1 in Mexico City and Sao Paulo.

The 18-year-old became the first driver to be signed to the German manufacturer's programme earlier this year and dovetailed his duties with a campaign in F3 where he finished runner up with Trident Motorsport.

He'll step up to F2 next season with Invicta Racing as part of his development, with the two runs in FP1 in Mexico and Brazil giving him valuable on-track experience.

“Getting behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car at a Grand Prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid," said Slater.

"I’ve learned a lot this year, and these Free Practice outings with Audi Revolut F1 Team will be another opportunity to keep gaining on-track experience.

"Being part of the Audi Driver Development Programme has already given me some incredible opportunities, and I am grateful for their trust and support.

"I’m really looking forward to getting out on track: my focus will be on doing the best job I can, helping the team with its programme and taking as many learnings as possible from both sessions.”

Audi Racing Director and Audi Driver Development Programme Director Allan McNish added: "We have seen Freddie making great progress throughout recent years, both on and off the track; it is the right time for Freddie to step up.

"These appearances in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development before he steps up to Formula 2 next season.

"We are looking forward to seeing him in the R26 and supporting him through these two important FP1 sessions."

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 United States GP
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend as Austin hosts Round 18 on the calendar, the United States Grand Prix.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, October 23, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, October 24, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, October 25.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 1959 (Sebring)

Track Length – 5.513km

Lap record – 1m 36.169s, Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, 2019

Most pole positions – Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton (4)

Most wins – Lewis Hamilton (6)

Trivia – In 2022, Austin set a then F1 record with a three-day attendance of around 440,000 fans

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 230 metres

Overtakes completed in 2025 – 71

Safety Car probability – 29%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 43%*

Pit stop time loss – 19.90 seconds

*From the last seven races in Austin

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: The Circuit of The Americas is a great track that takes inspiration from parts of other legendary corners on the calendar.

The uphill Turn 1 is difficult at the race start as there are loads of different lines that can be taken, then you sweep through the first sector, which is a bit like Silverstone, where you’re trying to find your rhythm.

After that, it’s the long back straight and you’ve got to get your braking point right at the end of it…

Probably the hardest section on the circuit is Turn 13 through to Turn 15, which feels like an odd complex of corners behind the wheel. Turn 13 is conventional, but finding your line through to 15 is not easy, while that Turn 14 area puts a lot of load on the tyres.

You go through the quadruple right-hander after that, followed by Turn 19, which is a really nice corner – though track limits are an issue.

Finally, you stop for Turn 20, then it’s a short burst to the line, but drivers need to be careful not to light things up as it’s easy to break traction.

Everything you need to know about the Circuit of The Americas

Last five United States GP polesitters

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2023 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2022 – Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Last five United States GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Tyre and strategy insight

“The Austin circuit, which is 5.513 kilometres long, features a mix of high-speed corners, rapid direction changes and slower sections that demand strong traction,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview, with the tyre selection for the event seeing the C2 used as the hard, the C3 as the medium and the C4 as the soft.

“To be competitive, teams must combine good straight-line speed with efficient aerodynamic load through the more technical sections, an aspect that becomes even more important with the current generation of Formula 1 cars.

“From a tyre perspective, COTA places demands on both axles. In the first sector, characterised by fast corners and direction changes inspired by some of Europe’s great circuits, the front tyres will be placed under particular stress. In the third sector, meanwhile, the numerous acceleration zones out of slow corners will tend to generate thermal degradation primarily on the rear tyres.

“The asphalt surface is not particularly abrasive. A section of the circuit between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced earlier this year. However, the ageing effect on the remainder of the track continues to be significant and contributes to high wear levels. Tyre wear, rather than graining, could therefore prove to be one of the key factors over the weekend. During last year's event, several tyres reached very high wear values.

“Track grip is generally good, aided by the support categories, including the Porsche Carrera Cup North America, which has been supplied by Pirelli since the start of this year. Track evolution, on the other hand, has traditionally not been among the most pronounced on the calendar.

“From a strategic standpoint, the presence of the C2 as the hard compound could favour long stints, offering teams a solid option for what is likely to be a one-stop race. However, the high temperatures that typically characterise the Texan weekend must also be taken into account, as they could increase degradation and open the door to alternative strategies.”

Current form

As has been the case since Round 3 in Japan, Kimi Antonelli remains at the top of the drivers’ standings – but this weekend marks the first in which the Italian has a mathematical chance of sealing his maiden title.

For this to happen, Antonelli would need to win the race with Mercedes team mate George Russell finishing ninth or lower and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton placing no higher than fifth. Can the 20-year-old become the youngest-ever World Champion in Austin?

While Antonelli and the Silver Arrows continue to head the standings, it is Max Verstappen and Red Bull who have been leading the way on track at the last two rounds, the Dutchman scoring back-to-back victories in Malaysia and Singapore.

Verstappen holds a strong record at the Circuit of The Americas, having triumphed in four of F1’s last five visits to the track – and the four-time World Champion will doubtless be keen to add to that run.

Elsewhere, McLaren will be hoping for a stronger weekend after Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s clash in the Singapore Sprint, while Ferrari also experienced mixed fortunes in Marina Bay, with Charles Leclerc securing a podium result as Hamilton slipped backwards following a backfired strategy.

Behind them, Racing Bulls have further strengthened their hold on P5 in the midfield battle – now holding an advantage of 32 points over sixth-placed Alpine – while Haas arrive into the event days after confirming that rookie Rafael Camara will join the team in 2027.

Iconic moment

The inaugural Austin race back in 2012 was an exhilarating watch, with Lewis Hamilton chasing down Red Bull’s Sebastian Vettel in his McLaren.

After Vettel lost momentum behind a backmarker, Hamilton sensed his opportunity to pounce for the lead – and the Briton duly took his chance.

title: Everything you need to know about the Circuit of The Americas
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season heads to Texas this weekend for the United States Grand Prix, as Austin’s Circuit of The Americas prepares to welcome the drivers for Round 18 of the campaign. But how much do you know about the famous American venue? F1.com has your all-in-one guide…

Key Circuit of The Americas statistics

Circuit length: 5.513km

Number of turns: 20

Number of laps: 56

Race distance: 308.405km

Lap record: 1m 36.169s – Charles Leclerc (2019)

When was Austin’s first Grand Prix?

The Circuit of The Americas made its Formula 1 debut in 2012, becoming the first purpose-built F1 venue in the United States and marking the championship’s return to the country after a five-year absence.

It was designed by renowned circuit architect Hermann Tilke and the track takes inspiration from some of F1’s most famous corners, including Silverstone’s Maggots and Becketts sequence and the sweeping turns in the stadium section of Hockenheim in Germany.

The inaugural race was won by Lewis Hamilton, who overtook Sebastian Vettel to claim his final victory for McLaren before his switch to Mercedes. The Briton has since become the most successful F1 driver in COTA’s history, with five victories to his name.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

The 5.513km circuit combines high-speed changes of direction with tight, technical corners. Meanwhile, the steep uphill approach to Turn 1 and blind apex offers one of the most dramatic starts to a lap anywhere on the calendar.

With 20 corners and several overtaking opportunities, drivers need to balance speed and precision throughout the lap, particularly through the opening sector and the more technical final sector.

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver, explained: “The Circuit of The Americas is a great track that takes inspiration from parts of other legendary corners on the calendar.

“The uphill Turn 1 is difficult at the race start as there are loads of different lines that can be taken, then you sweep through the first sector, which is a bit like Silverstone, where you’re trying to find your rhythm.

“After that, it’s the long back straight and you’ve got to get your braking point right at the end of it.

“Probably the hardest section on the circuit is Turn 13 through to Turn 15, which feels like an odd complex of corners behind the wheel. Turn 13 is conventional, but finding your line through to 15 is not easy, while that Turn 14 area puts a lot of load on the tyres.

“You go through the quadruple right-hander after that, followed by Turn 19, which is a really nice corner – though track limits are an issue.

“Finally, you stop for Turn 20, then it’s a short burst to the line, but drivers need to be careful not to light things up as it’s easy to break traction."

"The Circuit of The Americas is a great track that takes inspiration from parts of other legendary corners on the calendar."Jolyon Palmer

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

In Austin, there are two designated Straight Mode zones – the first is located between Turns 11 and 12, while the second runs along the start/finish straight after Turn 20 into Turn 1.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

Around the Circuit of The Americas, the Overtake Detection point comes as drivers head out of Turn 20, while the Overtake Activation line follows on the start/finish straight.

Five fun facts about the United States Grand Prix

Everything really is bigger in Texas! For 2026, COTA is unveiling what is set to be the world’s largest cowboy hat, measuring 75 feet long, with a themed bar underneath. The attraction will be located in the circuit’s Lone Star Land fan area.

Lewis Hamilton has clinched two of his seven World Drivers’ Championships at COTA, securing his third title in 2015 and his sixth in 2019.

Before Austin took over in 2012, five other circuits hosted the United States Grand Prix – Sebring, Riverside, Watkins Glen, Phoenix and Indianapolis.

F1 ACADEMY will return to COTA this year for the first time since its inaugural season in 2023, with the series set to stage three races across the weekend.

Mercedes hold the record for the most wins in COTA with five victories to date, while Red Bull are close behind with four.

title: Lewis Hamilton 'forced' to delay F1 retirement after major decision
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has suggested he will continue to race in F1 until at least the sport makes its return to Africa.

F1 confirmed last week that it will return to the African continent in the early 2030s, with Rwanda joining the calendar for the first time.

Hamilton has long battled for an African event on the schedule, with the region last hosting a race in 1993 at Kyalami in South Africa.

Should Rwanda join the calendar in 2030 at the earliest, Hamilton will be 45 years of age and entering his 24th F1 campaign.

But the seven-time champion insists he is determined to do so, stating he will work to ensure he can still compete at a high level over the coming years.

"I'm now forced to have to stay longer because we have a race in Africa, that's been my dream to be able to race in Africa," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

"I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can.

"If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton had 'countless meetings' to ensure African return

Rwanda was one of several locations in Africa that voiced interest in joining the F1 schedule in recent years.

Hamilton highlighted that he played his part in getting the continent back on the calendar, having had many meetings with key personnel.

"I've been advocating for a race in Africa for many, many, many years.

"Countless meetings with the stakeholders, so many meetings with Stefano at his office in London, but also at race weekends.

"Countless calls. 'What's happening? Where are we going? Who are we meeting with?' Many meetings with different presidents from different countries.

"Lots of phone calls with different presidents from different countries within Africa.

"For me, it's a place that deserves to have a grand prix. It's more about it's more than just about one country.

"It's about the continent in itself, and there are so many beautiful countries within it, and the people are so lovely.

"The culture is so rich, and I think it's important that we get to show that to the world, and we get to do that with our sport."

title: Fernando Alonso addresses surprise Dakar test after denying race entry
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has insisted that his recent Dakar Rally test outing does not mean he will be competing in the 2027 edition of the event.

Earlier this month, the Spaniard insisted that it would be "impossible" to prepare for the Dakar Rally in January while also gearing up for another F1 campaign.

However, shortly after the comments were made, Alonso was spotted in Morocco with Prodrive, behind the wheel of a black-liveried car.

It sparked suggestions that Alonso's original comments may not have been genuine, but the two-time champion insisted that a Dakar entry is not on the cards for next year.

"Every week, I'm in a race car," Alonso told media including RacingNews365.

"I do a lot of karting, and there are no rumours that I will do the world championship. I drove in Barcelona with [Ayrton] Senna's car, and I was not doing the historic Grand Prix at any point.

"I love driving cars, and that's the nature of myself."

[Article continues below]

Alonso: Dakar cannot be more different to F1

Alonso has competed at Dakar before, entering the race in 2020 for the first time during a stint away from the F1 schedule.

Having experienced what it takes to compete in the lengthy event, Alonso reiterated his stance that he will not be able to balance both F1 and Dakar.

"Dakar, after I did it in 2020, it was the most difficult challenge for me, for an F1 driver.

"It cannot be more different than F1 in terms of driving techniques and how to read the terrain, the way you drive the car with both feet, brake and throttle all the time to stabilise the car, and this kind of thing.

"It's completely the opposite of F1, so that's why it's appealing.

"But it is difficult to fit, especially in the same year, both challenges of F1 and Dakar."

title: Franco Colapinto explains 'last act' behind 'hate side' condemnation video
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto released a video statement following the Singapore GP urging for an end to online abuse from his fanbase.

22 October 8:25PM

Franco Colapinto has revealed he felt releasing a video statement was the "last thing" he could do to try to halt a wave of online abuse directed at fellow drivers and his own Alpine mechanics and engineers from the "hate side" of his own fanbase.

The Argentine's video, posted on his social media channels after Singapore, followed a season in which Alpine has repeatedly had to intervene over the conduct of parts of Colapinto's fanbase.

Some supporters attached to Colapinto's rapid rise have used the driver's online platforms to direct hostile and abusive messages at rival drivers, as well as at the mechanics and engineers working directly with Colapinto at Alpine.

Colapinto said he felt compelled to act personally after witnessing the toll the abuse was taking on people close to him within the team.

Discussing why he released a video statement, Colapinto told select media, including RacingNews365: "I love this sport. First of all, I'm very grateful to all the fans supporting me, and I think in every sport and every fan base, there's a bad side, the hate side, and people posting bad comments that don't help athletes perform at their best."

"To me, it crossed a few lines lately. I talked a lot about it, and I think it was probably the last thing I could do to make a statement. Me talking and making a video like that was always going to be positive, so I was keen to do it.

"Especially as my mechanics and engineers also got a lot of hate. These are people from my team who want me to do well and help me perform, and I'm working with them daily, yet they're getting these kinds of messages.

"It just hurts me in general, and of course, other drivers are receiving them as well. But that's something we talk about constantly. I've been talking about it for the last 10 races, probably."

Driver

Franco Colapinto

Argentine

43

Max Verstappen also urging for end of online abuse in motorsport

Alpine has already issued multiple public statements across the campaign addressing the issue, including an open letter in April following flashpoints in China and Japan involving Colapinto, and a further condemnation after September's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, when a safety car restart crash eliminated Lando Norris and Pierre Gasly and triggered a fresh torrent of abuse.

That wave of hostility, according to reports at the time, targeted Norris, team personnel and members of the media.

The issue has not been confined to Colapinto's fanbase. Max Verstappen also released a statement condemning online abuse after his GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup outing at Portimao, where his teammate Chris Lulham was targeted following an on-track collision that led to a drive-through penalty.

Colapinto pointed to that intervention as evidence of a wider problem spreading across the sport.

"So I do my best," continued Colapinto. "I think, again, it kept crossing some lines. So the last thing I thought I could do was make a video, and I think it helped.

"You saw Max make a statement about it as well. So, again, it's happening a lot, and there is an issue with that in sport nowadays, as well as in many different areas: music artists, actors, it's everywhere.

"The entity that we try to give is personal. On my side, it doesn't hurt me too much because I don't look at it too much. I don't put too much tension on it, and I don't give it too much importance. But for some, it does, and we need to pay attention to it and improve the situation. So hopefully it does."

Franco Colapinto hopeful video statement will improve online abuse situation

Unfortunately, Colapinto's own team have been targeted on several occasions, a further line crossed in his eyes.

Asked whether the abuse towards his engineers and mechanics was also taking place online, Colapinto replied: "Well, I don't have their phones. Honestly, I don't know. But from what I understand, they received messages and comments. It just, again, crossed the line.

"I don't want to talk about this too much. I talked about it on my social media, and I'm talking about it now. It's again something that I want to stop talking about every weekend. That's why I also read a statement: to focus on racing and not be talking about this constantly.

"But I hope it helps. Again, for me, it crossed a couple of lines lately, and the last thing I could do was this, and hopefully it improves the situation slightly."

title: Max Verstappen statistic triggering ‘sense of resignation’ among F1 rivals
excerpt:
Max Verstappen is searching for a third consecutive victory this weekend, to continue his sensational run of form.

A single statistic highlighted by Jolyon Palmer shows just how relentless Max Verstappen has been since the Monaco Grand Prix, with the four-time champion triggering a "sense of resignation" among the rest of the F1 grid, in the eyes of the former Renault driver.

Verstappen trailed championship leader Kimi Antonelli by 113 points after the Monaco round, the sixth race of the season.

But in the 11 races completed since, the Red Bull driver has lost just six points to the Mercedes driver in the standings battle, a run of form Palmer says underlines how dominant Verstappen has been with a car that has steadily improved behind him.

Speaking on the F1 Nation podcast, Palmer pointed to the scale of Red Bull's turnaround in 2026 as central to the story.

"I think that's the incredible thing when you look at the whole picture here: the uptrend for Red Bull is massive," Palmer said. "We've spoken for years about McLaren's turnaround in form.

"A couple of years ago, certainly, it was huge when Lando came from being nowhere to suddenly making us think, 'Can he fight for a championship?' before he did.

"But I think this Red Bull turnaround in form might be, on paper, the biggest, when you look at the percentage difference, if they can cement it through these final races.

"And when you look at Max, he's been delivering at a high level all season. It's not a massive surprise. There have been one or two mistakes, which, for once this year, have shown us that he's human, but generally, his level is still extremely high."

The staggering numbers behind Max Verstappen's 2026 recovery

Palmer then turned to the numbers behind Verstappen's recovery, framing them as evidence of a driver operating on a different plane to the rest of the grid.

"And I was looking through it," added Palmer. "After six races, after Monaco, he was 113 points behind Kimi Antonelli. In the 11 races since, he's lost six points to Kimi.

"If you started the championship after Monaco, Max would be champion. Probably, if you started it before Monaco, by the end of the season, he'd have enough points to be champion.

"That's the incredible form that he's shown when he didn't have the fastest car, and now he does. He's formidable, and I still just think he's got, in terms of driving, I think he's got everyone else almost fearing the battle with him. There's almost a sense of resignation when you take on Max from the rest of the field."

Antonelli still leads the drivers' championship on 340 points after 17 rounds, with Verstappen fourth on 221, behind George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

But with six races remaining, starting at the United States Grand Prix this weekend, Palmer's numbers suggest the momentum lies firmly with the Dutchman.

title: Sergio Perez reveals influence of 'second father' in F1 career
excerpt:
The influence of Mexican billionaire Carlos Slim on Sergio Perez's career has been phenomenal.

Sergio Perez has described Mexican billionaire Carlos Slim as his "second father", crediting him with shaping virtually every stage of his Formula 1 career.

Perez's relationship with the Slim family dates back to his childhood, when his father, Antonio Perez Garibay, worked in motorsport promotion alongside Mexican racer Adrian Fernandez.

That connection eventually brought the young Perez into Escuderia Telmex, the driver development programme founded in 2002 by the Slim family to support Mexican and Latin American racing talent.

Telmex funding paid for Perez's move to Europe as a teenager to race in Formula BMW, and continued through his rise via British Formula 3 and GP2.

When Perez graduated to Formula 1 with Sauber in 2011, that backing came with him: Telmex signed a commercial partnership with the Swiss team alongside his race contract, bringing sponsorship from America Movil brands such as Telmex, Telcel and Claro.

That support has followed Perez through Sauber, McLaren, Force India, Racing Point and Red Bull, with Escuderia Telmex functioning less as a traditional management agency and more as a long-term personal backing project tied directly to the Mexican driver.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Sergio Pérez

Mexican

11

Perez - 'My biggest supporter'

Reflecting on that support, Perez left no doubt about its significance.

"Obviously, they have been super important to me," said Perez, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

"Without Carlos, I wouldn't be here. He's been my biggest supporter since I was very young. Not just in terms of financial support. He's basically my second father because he's really followed my career, really followed me personally.

"He's a really close friend of mine. He knows everything that's going on in my life, and he has always given me very good advice throughout my career."

The 36-year-old Cadillac driver will get another reminder of his home support next weekend, when F1 heads to Mexico City for what will be his 300th grand prix start.

Asked whether he was bracing himself for the occasion, Perez replied: "Yeah, especially as I wasn't there last year.

"This year, I'm really looking forward to it. We're doing a road show on the Wednesday before.

"It's my 300th race as well at home, so it's pretty incredible that all of this is happening in Mexico. [I am] Super, super happy and so much looking forward to it."

title: Aston Martin confirm Mexico City first practice driver replacement
excerpt:
Lance Stroll will be replaced in first practice at next weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Aston Martin has confirmed that third driver Jak Crawford will take over Lance Stroll's AMR26 for first practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The session at the Autódromo Hermános Rodríguez will be Crawford's fourth FP1 appearance of the season, completing the team's quota of mandatory rookie outings for 2026.

The announcement by Aston Martin was made ahead of Crawford's home race weekend in Austin, with him in the United States Grand Prix paddock to continue supporting the team.

The American will arrive in Mexico City almost exactly a year on from his Formula 1 practice debut, which also came at the same circuit back in 2025.

Since that first outing, the 21-year-old has kept building his case for a future race seat, racking up further race weekend appearances alongside extensive testing and simulator work. His technical feedback and growing experience behind the wheel have continued to impress the team.

Jak Crawford eyes special Mexico City F1 appearance

"I'm really looking forward to getting back behind the wheel of the AMR26 in Mexico City," said Crawford.

"It's a special circuit for me as it's where I made my FP1 debut last year, so it's great to return with more experience under my belt. I've learned a lot through my time on track and in the simulator this season, and I'm looking forward to putting that into practice.

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack explained why the team was keen to hand Crawford another run in the car.

"We are pleased to give Jak another opportunity in the AMR26," said Krack.

title: Mercedes 'big concern' triggers troubling question: 'How are they even going to fight?'
excerpt:
Mercedes has dominated both F1 championships this year, despite the W17 no longer having the stranglehold on victories it enjoyed at the start of the season — but a looming question hangs over the team heading into 2027.

Jolyon Palmer has questioned whether Mercedes will even be in F1 title contention next season, given the rate of improvement from rival teams.

Palmer feels the Brackley-based squad's trajectory over the current campaign is a "big concern", with Ferrari, McLaren and now Red Bull challenging — and beating — the once-dominant W17.

When the new era of F1 regulations kicked off with the year-opening Australian Grand Prix, Mercedes comfortably had the measure of the field.

Together, George Russell and Kimi Antonelli won the first six rounds of the season, leaving the eight-time constructors' champions cruising to another title.

However, the chasing pack has closed in, and Mercedes' recent upgrade has failed — so far — to bring the expected performance gains to re-establish its once-healthy advantage.

With F1 returning to the traditional weekend format for the United States Grand Prix after the final sprint event of the year in Singapore, Palmer believes it is the perfect chance for the Toto Wolff-led team to get back on track.

"Three practices for us to get into — I like an old-school weekend," the former Renault driver said on the F1 Nation podcast. "The teams and drivers need it.

"It's Mercedes [that needs it] more than anyone to understand their car. But I look up and down the field, and there are a few others; I look at McLaren, who still have to troubleshoot some issues...

"But Mercedes is at an opportune moment to fully move forward with this car. And when you look at the trajectory of the team from the start of the year to now — it's a big concern for them."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Jolyon Palmer

British

The looming question hanging over Mercedes

17 rounds into the season, Mercedes has racked up 11 victories, whilst Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have two apiece.

It leaves the Silver Arrows with a 134-point lead over the Scuderia in the standings, one that is unlikely to be overtaken with only five or six rounds — due to the uncertainty surrounding Qatar and Abu Dhabi — remaining.

With both titles surely wrapped up, Palmer highlighted the need to turn attention towards 2027 and get to grips with the car, or face a bleak campaign next term.

He added: "How are they going to even fight for the championship next year with the way that everyone has caught and perhaps surpassed them?

"So their number one goal for the rest of the year — the titles are in the pocket — has to now be — it doesn't matter if you don't even win a race — understand the car and make sure that you find out that when you put parts into development back at Brackley, when you put them on the car, you go quicker.

"That is the key now to Mercedes' future success. That the current success is in the bag."

title: Renault agrees sale of former F1 engine headquarters
excerpt:
Renault Group has agreed to sell Alpine Racing SAS, the Formula 1 engine operation based at the historic Viry-Châtillon site near Paris, to Belgian powertrain specialist Dumarey Group.

According to Reuters, the deal preserves 150 jobs at the facility, which has been at the centre of the French manufacturer's works engine programme for decades.

Financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed.

The sale comes two years after Renault decided, in 2024, to pull out of building its own F1 power units, instead switching the Alpine team to customer Mercedes engines from 2026 onwards.

Once the deal is completed, Alpine Racing SAS will operate fully under the Dumarey brand, with the Belgian group taking over both ownership and management of the site.

Renault and Dumarey said the move could open the door to the Viry-Châtillon operation supplying its Formula 1 engine expertise to other racing teams in the future.

Dumarey chairman and founder Guido Dumarey said the takeover was about safeguarding the site's technical knowledge rather than winding it down.

"Our ambition is to preserve and further develop this exceptional engineering expertise while creating new opportunities for growth," Dumarey said in a statement.

title: Audi hands rising star two major F1 chances as debut confirmed
excerpt:
Formula 1 will have a new face in first practice next weekend in Mexico City.

Freddie Slater will make his Formula 1 debut with Audi next weekend, taking part in first practice at both the Mexico City and Sao Paulo Grands Prix.

The 18-year-old became the first driver signed to the Audi driver development programme earlier this year, and the two FP1 outings mark a significant step in his progression towards the grid.

Slater has just completed a strong rookie season in Formula 3 with Trident Motorsport, finishing runner-up in the championship.

He claimed eight podiums across eight consecutive weekends, three pole positions and one feature race win, and remained in title contention until the finale in Madrid in September.

The Briton will move up to Formula 2 with Invicta Racing in 2027, and the FP1 sessions in Mexico and Brazil are intended to add further on-track experience ahead of that step.

His appearances also form part of the team's wider commitment to giving young drivers track time in Formula 1, in line with FIA regulations.

Team

Audi

Freddie Slater set for 'realisation of a childhood dream'

Audi racing director and head of the Audi driver development programme, Allan McNish, said Slater had earned his chance after a strong campaign.

"We have seen Freddie making great progress throughout recent years, both on and off the track; it is the right time for Freddie to step-up," McNish said.

"These appearances in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development before he steps up to Formula 2 next season.

"We are looking forward to seeing him in the R26 and supporting him through these two important FP1 sessions."

Slater himself described the opportunity as the realisation of a childhood dream, with it to be watched with much anticipation.

"Getting behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car at a Grand Prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I've been dreaming of since I was a kid," Slater said.

"I've learned a lot this year, and these free practice outings with Audi will be another opportunity to keep gaining on-track experience.

"Being part of the Audi driver development programme has already given me some incredible opportunities, and I am grateful for their trust and support.

"I'm really looking forward to getting out on track: my focus will be on doing the best job I can, helping the team with its programme and taking as many learnings as possible from both sessions."

title: Stunned Max Verstappen yanked from F1 cooldown room as podium revoked
excerpt:
In 2017, Max Verstappen appeared to be heading for third place in the United States after a mind-blowing pass on Kimi Räikkönen on the final lap. Nothing could have been further from the truth...

Nine years ago, the Circuit of the Americas delivered one of the most dramatic finishes of Max Verstappen's early career.

At the 2017 United States Grand Prix, the Dutchman, then just 19, appeared to have pulled off a stunning last-lap move to claim third place. The celebrations lasted only a few minutes.

Verstappen had started that race from P16 on the grid after picking up a grid penalty for exceeding his allocation of power unit components.

A sharp strategy and strong race pace helped him carve through the field, and by the closing stages he had Kimi Räikkönen in his sights in the battle for the final podium spot.

On the 56th and final lap, Verstappen pounced at Turn 17. He dived down the inside of the Finn, running all four wheels wide of the white line at the edge of the circuit.

The move handed him third place across the line, a piece of overtaking that briefly had the paddock buzzing, though it was always likely to draw scrutiny given where it had happened.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Penalty strikes

The stewards, as it turned out, took a dim view of the move. They ruled that Verstappen had gained a lasting advantage over Räikkönen by leaving the track, and handed him a five-second time penalty.

The complication was timing. The penalty was only confirmed after Verstappen had already made his way to the podium area.

He had been taken to the cooldown room, the space reserved for the top three finishers ahead of the trophy presentation, when the penalty was applied to his race time. It dropped him from third to fourth in the official classification, behind Räikkönen.

What followed was an awkward scene played out in front of the cameras: Verstappen was pulled out of the cooldown room on the spot to make way for Räikkönen, who was handed his podium place moments before the ceremony got underway.

It was not the first time Verstappen had been removed from the cooldown room in such circumstances. A year earlier, at the 2016 Mexican Grand Prix, the same thing had happened, with the then-teenager demoted after the fact to fourth place behind Daniel Ricciardo following a clash with Sebastian Vettel.

Lewis Hamilton won the 2017 race from pole position, controlling much of the Grand Prix after briefly losing the lead to Vettel on the opening lap before reclaiming it and cruising to his ninth win of that season.

Vettel finished second for Ferrari, with Räikkönen ultimately classified third and Verstappen fourth. Hamilton's victory, combined with Valtteri Bottas finishing fifth, was enough to seal Mercedes' fourth consecutive constructors' championship.

title: How F1 helps Kimi Antonelli avoid breaking the law in the United States
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli stands a good chance of finishing on the podium at the United States Grand Prix this weekend, but he cannot legally drink the champagne. So what does F1 do to keep drivers under the local drinking age from breaking the law?

Kimi Antonelli could celebrate becoming Formula 1 drivers' champion at this weekend's United States Grand Prix, but the Mercedes driver will have to make do without the traditional champagne.

The 20-year-old Italian heads to the Circuit of the Americas with a 102-point championship lead over team-mate George Russell, with an opportunity to secure his maiden drivers' crown.

Even if he does not clinch the title but reaches the podium in Austin, he will have to make do with breaking from tradition.

Antonelli remains below the legal drinking age of 21 in the United States, meaning F1 must provide an alcohol-free alternative.

What will Kimi Antonelli drink on the Austin F1 podium?

Antonelli is expected to receive a non-alcoholic substitute, potentially sparkling rose water, rather than the Moët & Chandon champagne traditionally used during podium celebrations.

The precise beverage has not been confirmed, although F1 already has procedures for accommodating drivers who cannot legally consume alcohol.

The Mercedes driver encountered the same situation after winning the Miami Grand Prix in May, when he was 19.

Antonelli celebrated with an unbranded bottle containing a non-alcoholic drink, allowing him to participate in the customary podium spraying.

© XPBimages

Which F1 countries have higher legal drinking ages?

The United States has a minimum drinking age of 21, meaning Antonelli will face the same restriction at the Las Vegas Grand Prix and at Miami again in 2027, when he will still be 20.

Japan also presented a problem earlier this season, when Antonelli was 19 and below its legal drinking age of 20.

Other young drivers can face similar restrictions, including Arvid Lindblad, who is still only 19. However, the Racing Bulls driver has yet to reach the F1 rostrum.

Which F1 grands prix do not use champagne?

Alcohol is not used during podium ceremonies at the Bahrain, Saudi Arabian, Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix, where rose water is traditionally sprayed instead.

These arrangements reflect local cultural and religious considerations and apply to every driver, regardless of age.

Consequently, even established champions such as Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton must swap champagne for an alcohol-free alternative at those events.

For Antonelli, however, Austin could provide the unusual spectacle of a newly crowned world champion celebrating one of motorsport's greatest achievements without being legally old enough to drink champagne.

title: Departing F1 driver tells sport where to go with future rules
excerpt:
Outgoing F1 driver Esteban Ocon has offered a novel solution to the sport's future engine debate following the heavy criticism that has shrouded the current season.

F1's hybrid power units have faced sustained criticism this year for the severe energy derate drivers experience on straights when batteries deplete, sometimes dropping from over 1,000 horsepower to around 550 horsepower.

The current regulations split power roughly 52:48 between a 1.6-litre turbocharged V6 producing around 400 kW, and a 350 kW electric motor, after the costly MGU-H was scrapped to cut costs and attract new manufacturers such as Audi.

But the system has drawn fire from teams and drivers alike over time, notably over extreme closing-speed differences and the need for lift-and-coast energy harvesting through corners, prompting the FIA to review the deployment parameters.

Ocon, who leaves Haas at the end of this season after two years with the team but is hopeful of staying in F1 in some capacity for 2027, even if a reserve role proves necessary, has floated an unconventional alternative when discussing the engine debate.

"We're all thinking about V8s, V10s, obviously naturally aspirated," said Ocon, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "That's probably the best drivability you can get.

"But with Formula 1 nowadays, the amount of power we get, we might be lacking a bit of torque on the bottom end. And that's where the hybrid technology comes into play, and that's where it fills the lack of torque that this engine would have.

"So I think the best supercars in the market are the ones with a loud engine filled with a bit of electric.

"Or you don't go electric at all, and you put turbos on it, like two, one small, one big, so you feel the lag at the bottom end.

"But on a race car, I haven't seen many biturbo winning machines, so it would be quite interesting.

"Anyway, I think there are so many possibilities on the engine side and possibilities that could be better than what we have now."

[Article continues below]

Alonso urges pragmatism

Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, who raced in F1 during the V8 and V10 eras before the sport turned to turbo-hybrids, struck a more measured tone when asked about reverting to the old formula.

"The world has changed," the Spaniard said.

"Obviously, they were fun cars to drive, very light, very loud, but maybe they don't fit with today's world, that kind of technology.

"And we were changing engines when I started. We had an engine for Saturday, 12 laps in quali, and then an engine for Sunday. So is that possible in today's world? Probably not.

"We need to be happy and adapt to the world, and maybe the hybrid systems are the way to go.

"We just need to find the ratio of the combustion and electric parts, how much we need to help on the electric side."

title: Max Verstappen offers old-fashioned solution to 'deciding lap time' in F1
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has called for Formula 1 to strip away the layers of energy management that now shape every lap, arguing the sport has strayed too far from the basics of driving.

Four-time F1 champion Verstappen has been among the most vocal critics of the current power unit regulations, which scrapped the MGU-H and pushed the MGU-K's output to 350 kW as part of a near 50/50 split between combustion and electrical power.

The change was designed to draw new manufacturers into the sport and boost road relevance, but it has also forced drivers into heavy energy conservation, including lifting, downshifting on straights and managing battery deployment rather than simply racing flat out.

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, the Red Bull explained that even routine moments on track, such as pulling away at the start, have become complicated by the software running in the background.

"The start-up procedure can take four or five seconds," said Verstappen. "Then normally you can just drive off.

"The problem is there is all the software in the background that can make you not pull away, or there is a glitch, or whatever. Even on slow laps, there's stuff that can happen.

"When you cross the line, you should be able to lift off and not worry about charging your battery or making sure that it's hitting the top of the pack at the right time.

"Or at the start as well, being sure that the battery is in the right place, and in an overtake, that the battery needs to be in the right place.

"You shouldn't be thinking about where to lift off, or to go down the gear to make sure that you have better deployment."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen - 'Not what racing should be about'

Verstappen went on to argue that such calculations have no place in the sport at its purest.

"All these kinds of things, that's not what racing should be about," said Verstappen. "You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and a throttle pedal, and that's what decides the lap time."

Verstappen's comments come after the FIA and power unit manufacturers were forced into a mid-season intervention, adjusting deployment and boost parameters after driver feedback and simulator work flagged dramatic closing speeds and cars slowing abruptly on full-throttle straights.

The FIA has since agreed phased adjustments over the next two seasons, moving to a 60-40 split in 2028, to rebalance future power units back toward the combustion engine.

For Verstappen, the appeal is straightforward: a simpler car, with lap time decided by driver input alone.

title: F1 paddock turned upside down after unexpected disqualifications — On This Day
excerpt:
Three years ago today, F1's classification sheet at Circuit of the Americas was torn up hours after the chequered flag, when Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were both thrown out of the 2023 United States Grand Prix for running illegal plank wear.

Max Verstappen had already done the hard work on track, taking his 50th career win despite battling brake trouble, fending off Lando Norris and holding firm as Hamilton charged through to apparent second place.

But Hamilton's result lasted only as long as it took the FIA to run its post-race checks.

Scrutineers found that both the Mercedes and the Ferrari breached Article 3.5.9 e) of the Technical Regulations, which governs the thickness of the plank fitted beneath the car's floor.

The regulation permits wear down to a minimum of 9.0mm from a baseline of 10.0mm, and both cars measured below that threshold.

The selection that changed the result

The FIA had picked Hamilton's and Leclerc's cars for physical inspection based on telemetry and performance data suggesting excessive bottoming during the race, Autosport reported. Once both failed, the FIA extended checks to Verstappen's and Norris's cars to establish whether the problem ran deeper. Those two passed.

Mercedes and Ferrari did not contest the measurements. Both teams pointed to COTA's notoriously bumpy surface and the sprint weekend format, which left just a single practice session to settle ride height before parc fermé locked everything in, according to The Race.

Ferrari's head of track engineering, Diego Ioverno, admitted the margin was wafer-thin. "Our car was below the minimum threshold by a few tenths [of a millimetre], but enough to bring the stewards to consider [our car] illegal," he said.

"With hindsight, rewinding the weekend, we may have lifted even more of the car, but we would have lost performance, and we are here always to try to optimise our own performance."

Leclerc, demoted from third to a non-score, took the outcome without complaint.

"The car was not touching at all, then obviously with high fuel, etc. Then you get to the race, and you get disqualified for the smallest margin possible," he explained. "But rules are rules, and they are written in black and white, so it's completely fair to be disqualified."

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff struck a similar tone, framing it as a lesson rather than an injustice.

"Others got it right where we got it wrong, and there's no wiggle room in the rules," he said. "We need to take it on the chin, do the learning, and come back stronger next weekend."

Hamilton, stripped of what would have been a strong recovery drive from third on the grid, called the outcome disappointing but not damning. "It is of course disappointing to be disqualified post-race, but that doesn't take away from the progress we've made this weekend," he said.

He later went further, suggesting the grid's issue was wider than two cars. "I have heard from different sources that there were many cars that had not been tested and were also illegal," Hamilton said. Nico Hülkenberg admitted he "might have been illegal myself," while Verstappen defended the wider field, pointing to the sprint format's single practice session as the root cause rather than any deliberate rule-bending.

[Article continues below]

Sargeant's solitary point

The disqualifications rippled all the way down the order. Norris was elevated to second, Carlos Sainz to third, and at the back of the points, Logan Sargeant was promoted to tenth, scoring the only point of his Formula 1 career.

"It's amazing to score my first point in F1 on home turf after the challenging weekend I've had," Sargeant said. "I'm so proud of this team and myself for the hard work and progress we've been making this season."

The American driver, dropped by Williams midway through the following season, never added to that solitary point.

The FIA's Tim Goss later explained why only two cars were checked that day rather than the whole field. "The check takes a while, and we found that they were the wrong side of the regulations. That caused us some concern," he said, adding that a full plank inspection requires partial disassembly taking roughly half an hour per car, making a grid-wide check impractical within race-day timeframes.

No regulation change followed directly from the Austin fallout, though the sprint parc fermé rules were loosened for 2024, splitting the window to give teams a setup adjustment between the sprint and qualifying, a shift widely linked in the paddock to the very trap that caught out Hamilton and Leclerc in Texas.

title: Mercedes detail latest F1 approach after unusual car experiment
excerpt:
Mercedes ran two different car specifications last time out in Singapore.

Mercedes has confirmed that it will run the upgraded specification of the W17 car in the United States this weekend.

Last time out in Singapore, only Kimi Antonelli used the fully upgraded car, while George Russell used the older version, allowing the team to compare both iterations.

The Brackley-based squad was defeated at the last two rounds in Malaysia and Singapore, with Red Bull and Max Verstappen taking back-to-back wins.

But as Mercedes closes in on a double title success this year, team principal Toto Wolff insisted it is not slowing down the development of its car.

"Malaysia and Singapore were difficult weekends for us and we have worked hard to understand where we fell short," he said.

"Austin gives us an opportunity to respond. We will run our latest update package on both cars as we continue to develop the car.

"The field is incredibly close, so we need to keep moving forward if we want to fight consistently at the front in the closing stages of the season."

Wolff sends Mercedes warning as double title success looms

Although the Silver Arrows have won the US Grand Prix five times since the start of the hybrid era, the team's last victory at the Circuit of the Americas came in 2019.

As Mercedes seeks to close out a strong season on a high note, Wolff insisted it can't afford to relax its approach.

"The United States Grand Prix begins another demanding triple-header," he said.

"There is plenty at stake, but we won't get ahead of ourselves.

"The priority is the weekend in front of us: execute well, maximise our performance and take each race as it comes."
